text: Thank you, Madam Chair. The subject site consists of an existing building located on the corner of Star Street and an unnamed laneway. The dwelling is proposed to contain four bedrooms, open living, kitchen, dining area, two bathrooms, a garage with car stacker and an upper level outdoor area. A new first floor bedroom is proposed to be constructed internally within the existing walls with a second floor is proposed to extend up from the first floor and provide a roofed north facing terrace. The maximum height of the dwelling is proposed to be 8.6 metres above the height of the existing footpath pavement at the southeast corner of the existing building. A new garage is also proposed to be built over the southern part of the vacant land to the west of the subject site. The new garage will accommodate two cars with an installed car lift. The site is located within the activity centre zone schedule one and is located within the heritage overlay HO 977. However, this building has no heritage significance, as well as being partially within the special building overlay, which is limited towards the southeast corner of the subject site. So the application has been assessed against the relevant planning policy framework, the municipal planning strategy, the zone particular and general provisions of the Greater Geelong Planning Scheme, where it is considered that the use of a dwelling is in keeping with the objectives of the precinct as it allows for accommodation uses. Consideration has also been given in relation to clause 54 for a single dwelling on the lot with the proposed development generally meeting the requirements within this clause. However, there are concerns regarding the car parking access to the site. The unnamed laneway that the car park will be accessed off is approximately three metres wide, with the garage entrance proposed to be four metres wide. So I'll just try to share my screen and play this recording. Sorry, just having a couple of technical issues bringing this up.

speaker: kyliegrzybek

speaker: leighpage
text: All right, no worries. So if everyone's seen it, that is fantastic. So in the video, the applicant has demonstrated that the turning movements using a Lexus 200 NT medium SUV. The length of that SUV is 4.63 metres with a width of 1.87 metres. The dimensions under the Australian standards for a standard B99 car, which is the size of vehicle that is required to be considered in this instance, is 5.2 metres in length. So that's a significant difference between what was used in that demonstrated video, which required five turning movements to access into that site. The lesser standard for that, which we don't consider, which is the B85 standard, the length of the car for that is 4.9 metres, which again is greater than what was used in that video demonstration. So that basically required five corrective movements to align the car within the garage and in the proposed stacker within the garage. It is noted in this video that the driver also needs to utilise the reversing cameras and aerial view perspective, as well as the front and rear parking beepers. And they are required to fully turn the steering wheel before each movement to access that area. This whole process shown in the video takes over sort of a minute and a half to actually access that car park. And depending on how the driver intends to exit the site, may need to reverse out into Star Street itself, if they don't manoeuvre into a position to be able to drive out in a forward direction. It is considered that under the Australian standards, three turning movements are acceptable when entering and exiting a car space. This has been clarified by VCAT, who have previously made a determination in 2017, that the intention of the Australian standard is to allow a single corrective manoeuvre. So that's up to four vehicle movements when entering or exiting a residential car space. This is to allow the car, these four movements is to allow the car to exit in a forward direction. The particular provision for car parking as set out under the decision guidelines within the planning scheme of this clause, seeks to ensure the ease and safety with which vehicles can access and circulate within the parking areas. As demonstrated by the submitted turning movements plan submitted by the applicant, the proposal requires approximately nine turning movements, which was based on the B99 standard, Australian standard to access and align a car within the garage. It is considered that given the number of movements, the access will create an unacceptable outcome and also creates a safety concern as there are no sight lines for vehicles exiting the site. Therefore, the recommendation was to refuse the application. Thank you.

text: Thank you. So the site is located on the southern side of Stephen Street, Newtown in a neighbourhood residential zone, Schedule 2 and within a heritage overlay, Schedule 2006. The site is occupied by an existing brick garage that historically was used as a stable for the building at the rear, fronting onto a Frasier Street. The proposal is for partial demolition of the existing garage and construction of a double storey dwelling at the rear. The dwelling has three bedrooms and has a maximum height of 7.3 metres. The existing garage is included within the heritage overlay, however, is not recognised as being significant. The application has required a planning permit under the zone for buildings and works, as the lot is less than 300 square metres and the heritage overlay on the site for partial demolition and buildings and works. The application was referred through to our heritage advisor, Dr David Rowe, who is supportive of the proposal and has noted that it provides a positive outcome in relation to the relevant heritage policy. The proposal was advertised by a sign on the site and letters to the adjoining properties. Following the notice period, the application received nine objections and one was later withdrawn, so the total number of objections is eight. No consultation meeting was held given the COVID situation, however, the applicant prepared a written response which was circulated to all of the objectors. The objections received relate to neighbourhood character and heritage issues, res code issues including overshadowing, overlooking site coverage, traffic issues and concern that the proposal may create a precedent for other sites within this area.
